content: Goiter refers to an abnormal enlargement of the thyroid gland. The presence of a goiter does not necessarily indicate thyroid dysfunction, as it can occur in individuals with hypothyroid, euthyroid, or hyperthyroid states. Globally, iodine deficiency is the most common cause of goiter. While goiters are typically painless, large goiters may cause compressive symptoms such as difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), difficulty breathing (dyspnea), and hoarseness of voice. Historical references to goiter date back to 2700 BC. In 1949, levothyroxine was successfully synthesized commercially, and in 1974, the World Health Organization (WHO) published the first histological classification of thyroid tumors, which has since been foundational for clinical, pathological, and epidemiological studies. Goiters can be classified based on etiological, epidemiological, anatomical, pathological, functional, and morphological factors. Disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis (TRH-TSH-thyroid hormone axis) can lead to structural and functional changes in the thyroid gland. A deficiency in thyroid hormone synthesis or intake triggers increased production of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which promotes thyroid gland hyperplasia and increased cellularity. Prolonged stimulation of this process results in goiter formation. The causes of goiter are multifactorial and include hereditary, hormonal, dietary, pharmacological, physiological, environmental, and pathological factors. Common causes include iodine deficiency, Graves' disease, and Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Genetic mutations in the thyroglobulin (Tg) gene, thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TSHR) gene, and sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) gene have also been implicated. Goiters present in various clinical forms, necessitating differentiation based on the specific subtype. The global incidence of goiter is approximately 1400–1700 per 100,000 females and 900 per 100,000 males. The prevalence of single thyroid nodules is around 3000 per 100,000 individuals worldwide. Goiters are more common in women over 45 years of age, with a female-to-male ratio of 4:1. There is no racial predilection for goiter. Risk factors for goiter include non-iodized salt consumption, age over 45 years, female gender, certain medications, and radiation exposure. Screening for goiter involves a physical examination, blood tests for free T4 and TSH levels, and imaging studies such as thyroid ultrasound, thyroid scans, and biopsy to rule out malignancy. Benign goiters typically exhibit slow nodule growth, while rapid growth and large size causing compressive symptoms may suggest thyroid cancer. Complications of goiter include those related to gland enlargement and thyroidectomy. The prognosis for benign goiter is generally favorable, but careful monitoring is recommended to detect potential malignancy. Radiation exposure has been linked to an increased risk of thyroid cancer. Symptoms of goiter include swelling at the base of the neck, difficulty swallowing, hoarseness of voice, and difficulty breathing. Physical examination often reveals neck swelling. Patients may be in a euthyroid, hypothyroid, or hyperthyroid state. Laboratory evaluation should include free T4, T3, TSH levels, and thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies. Plain neck X-rays may show tracheal deviation or compression and calcifications within the goiter. Ultrasound is useful for assessing thyroid gland characteristics and guiding fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC). Thyroid radioisotope scans can help determine functional activity, distinguishing nodules as hot, warm, or cold based on radioactive isotope uptake. Common isotopes used include iodine-123, technetium-99m, and iodine-131. Barium swallow studies may assess esophageal compression, and indirect laryngoscopy evaluates vocal cord mobility. Medical therapy for goiter aims to normalize hormone levels and treat inflammation. Treatment regimens may include Lugol’s iodine, antithyroid drugs, and beta-adrenergic blockers. Radioactive iodine may be used in cases of hyperactive thyroid glands. Thyroid surgery is indicated for compressive symptoms, hyperfunctioning thyroid, or thyroid cancer. Primary prevention of goiter includes iodine supplementation and smoking cessation. Secondary prevention measures are similar to primary prevention strategies.
